messages.subject: Controlling factors in regression
parts:
Dear all,

I am working on a particular morphological alternation in the Spanish verbal system and one of the factors that I am trying to test is the phonological form of the verb. The basic data frame has an outcome which is the morpheme, and as one of the predictors the verb on which the observation was made:

morph  Verb

X          verb1
Y          verb1
X          verb2
X          verb2
Y          verb1
Y          verb3
...

I took all the stems, converted them to phonemic transcription and built unigrams and bigrams with the phonemes in them. As a result I have some 200 new numeric factors (how many times the ngram is present in the stem) on which I can fit a random forest to predict the morpheme choice with relatively high accuracy. My problem is that there is already a high degree of lexical preferences by the alternation, so a simple logistic regression model with only "verb" as predictor has a higher accuracy than the random forest.

So my question is: is there any way to control for the effect of "verb" so that I am only testing phonological composition?

Thanks a lot!

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: [StatForLing with R] Controlling factors in regression
parts:
Seems to me like the problem is one of nested predictors, right? The
levels of the predictor VERB 100% predicts the 1-/2-gram predictors
perfectly and the 1-/2-gram predictors categorically rule out certain
verbs etc. I haven't seen many such cases so I might be off here but
maybe (big maybe!)

- you can treat both VERB and the 1-/2-gram predictors could be
treated as random effects, in which case you could define this nested
structure in the random-effects part of the formula
- mlogit in the same package allows to specify nested structures so
perhaps that can be used, too.

But again, I don't have much experience with that kind of stuff so
take the above with a bucket of salt and only as some very
first/tentative hints ...

Cheers,
STG

Dear Stefan,

thanks a lot for your answer. I had thought of nested predictors with lme4 but the model doesn't converge (it fails after working a couple of days). The only model that actually manages to handle all these predictors with nested effects are partition trees, and it seems the (some of the) effect remains :) So that was a great idea!

Best,

Matías
